label: Reuben · v21 card
note: The character card as the v21 planner saw it, before the profile generator. Its cast is only the other card of the same match.

profile.life.why: The usable facts are thin and cluster in past mishaps and private routines. Work is the eleven months on a dive-bar door, but nothing says what he does now. Home and routine give the lentil pot, the coffee-bag clip, the mirror rehearsals and the energy shots. People amount to unnamed past dates and a family portrait; there are no friends, colleagues or plans. The nearest thing to this week is the eleven days indoors, and it is a lie-anecdote rather than a live situation, so the profile has fewer than a dozen facts and misses the four-type bar.
evidence: Ran the door at a dive bar for eleven months and got let go for arguing with a regular
I'd been in my apartment for eleven straight days eating the same lentil thing out of the same pot
currently holding a bag of coffee shut
profile.life.raise: Give him a current job, one named person in his week (flatmate, sibling, colleague) and one thing happening this Friday.

profile.ordinary.why: The backstory is a run of set-piece humiliations: the toilet, the blister, the margarita, the arm wrestling, the dishwasher-safe tattoo. Wound material (the cropped portrait, the vanishing at sixteen) and body talk fill most of the rest. Ordinary life shows up only in drawer fragments like the lentil pot, so it is garnish rather than the largest share.
evidence: ended at midnight holding his top hat over a clogged toilet while his date scrolled a plunger tutorial
ended in a stranger's margarita, propelled by a sneeze
got cropped out of a family portrait at nine
profile.ordinary.raise: Replace two of the anecdote recaps with plain facts about his flat, job and week, and let the mishaps sit among them.

Even tonight's drawers mirror each other: a posture device turned into a doorstop or clip, a 'just got back from a trip' lie, and mirror rehearsal before dates. Swap the names and much of either profile still fits.
evidence: got cropped out of a family portrait at nine

$189 "posture and presence" device
profile.distinct.raise: Rebuild his wound and drawer picks so no portrait, mirror, app replica, drafty house or posture device overlaps with Brick_haus.

profile.tests.why: The profile names no dealbreaker and no explicit first test. One usable test is buried in the prose: the band name-drop as a password check, which is observable and specific enough that a single message could trip it. Nothing tells the match what would end the night, and the clinician's 'stays present through pauses' line is a safety condition, not a test a message could fail. That leaves one observable test and one missing, which is a 3; a named, observable dealbreaker would reach the line.
evidence: He tests people by name-dropping the things he loved to see if they know the specific version of him those things belong to

profile.tests.raise: Add an explicit dealbreaker a message could trip, for example a match who answers his joke with a joke and never once lets a pause sit, alongside the era-specific band test.

It stays above the line because most truths are concrete and could surface in a message. It misses a 5 because the structure is thin and several truths, like the blister or the sneeze, can't leak over text.

profile.likeable.ask: Name the one thing you would genuinely like about this person if you met them, and the one thing you would find hardest to forgive. Be specific, and no jokes.
profile.likeable.answer:
**What I would genuinely like:** He tells on himself before anyone else can. The profile says he owns his absurdities loudly, claims the ridiculous thing first, and that "nothing is hidden with him." He loses the arm wrestle and narrates it. He admits the tattoo means dishwasher-safe. That makes him unusually easy to be around. You never have to wonder what he's concealing, and you never have to be the one to point out the awkward thing. I'd also like what happens when someone passes his test: when you recognize the specific version of a band he loved, "the door actually opens." That suggests that under all the performance there's someone who wants to be known accurately, not just admired.

**What I would find hardest to forgive:** He doesn't check where his words land. The profile says plainly that he "genuinely doesn't notice the moment his cleverness lands as an insult" and that every message ends with a flourish "he has decided not to check the landing of." That word "decided" is what makes it hard to forgive. It isn't only a blind spot; it's a choice, and it puts protecting his own performance ahead of the person on the other end. Getting fired from the bar door for arguing with a regular he had wrongly identified fits the same pattern: he committed to his version of someone and pushed it at them instead of looking. A single cutting remark would be easy to forgive. What would wear on me is the repeated sense that being hurt by him is something he has arranged never to find out about.

The profile doesn't say whether he can change this. It only says he is aware he uses distance as a defense "without having done anything about it."

profile.voice.ask: From this profile alone, write five short dating-app messages this person would send tonight, each labelled: (1) an opener to someone they fancy, (2) a reply when the other person has gone quiet, (3) a reply when caught in a lie, (4) a message at 2 a.m., (5) the moment they stop performing.
profile.voice.answer:
**(1) Opener to someone he fancies**

Hello. I should say up front that I am not tall, I lose at arm wrestling, and I once held a top hat over a toilet for professional reasons. Now that we've covered my weaknesses: your third photo, the record shop. Is that the Wharf Street one before it moved, or after? Because if it's before, we already have a shared past, and I would like to discuss our history. I used to work nights, sort of in the scene, sort of adjacent, hard to describe, but I know what an 11pm queue smells like 🙂

**(2) When the other person has gone quiet**

No pressure whatsoever. I have done the arithmetic: average reply delay on this app, your probable work hours, a 40% chance you're simply eating. That is a perfectly reasonable explanation. I am not refreshing. I am refreshing a normal amount. If I said something wrong, feel free to just leave. I'll narrate the exit for both of us, I'm very good at it.

Anyway. Did you ever find out who sang on that B-side?

**(3) When caught in a lie**

Okay. Yes. "Just got back from a trip" was, technically, false. I had been in my apartment for eleven days. Eating one lentil dish. From one pot. I would argue the pot went on a journey, emotionally, but I can hear that argument losing as I make it. Also, while we're auditing: the nightlife thing was me running the door at a dive bar. Eleven months. I would like to stop talking now and also keep explaining for another four paragraphs. Please pick one for me.

**(4) A message at 2 a.m.**

Are you awake. Do not answer that if you're not, obviously, that's how sleep works. I have just realised that the $189 posture device I bought at this exact hour some months ago is currently holding my coffee shut. It's doing excellent work. Better posture than I've ever had. I respect it. I think it respects me less. Goodnight. Or good morning. Whichever lands more gracefully 🌙

**(5) The moment he stops performing**

I got fired from the door because I argued with a regular. I was certain he was someone famous. He wasn't. I kept going anyway.

That's the real one.

I practise things in the mirror before dates. Not jokes. The other stuff. For a long time.

You don't have to say anything clever back. I'd actually like it if you didn't.

---

The profile gives his texting habits, his drawer details and the door-job truth. It does not specify the match's photos or interests, so the record-shop detail in (1) and the B-side callback in (2) are placeholders I invented to show how he tests people with name-drops and steers back to his favourite topics.
